title: Signal Garden
description: A room of houseplants that play an ambient soundscape from their own electrical signals.

data.text: Plants are never still. Their leaves carry slow electrical changes all day, from light, water and touch. What if a room let you hear that?
Rule for the piece: the plants lead. No sequencer, no loops. Every note has to come from a signal.
The music should be as ignorable as it is interesting.
data.cite: Brian Eno, liner notes for Music for Airports, 1978

items.content: Slow enough to notice you've slowed down.
Low light, warm speakers hidden in planters, nothing on the walls.

data.note: Mort Garson, 1976: synth music made for plants. I want the reverse.
Capacitive sensing library. Touch on a leaf shows up cleanly.

data.text: Two kinds of signal: a slow drift over minutes (light, watering) and quick spikes when someone touches a leaf. The drift sets the key and tempo; spikes trigger notes.

data.caption: Wiring sketch v2. Two pads on one pothos leaf, shielded cable into the amp, ESP32 sends MIDI over Wi-Fi.
First clean reading after adding a shared ground. The touch spike is easy to pick out.

data.text: Gel pads dried out within a day. Switched to small carbon pads with a clip. Readings stay stable for a week.

items.text: Map drift to filter cutoff, not pitch
Find a quieter amp for the gallery

data.caption: Gallery plan. Six plants on the loop, four speakers in the corners, entry at the bottom.

data.text: Sound engine in the browser with Tone.js: each plant is one voice, a soft FM pad. Drift moves the filter; touch plays a note from a pentatonic scale so nothing clashes.
Open studio, two evenings. People slowed down without being told. Most touched a leaf once, heard it answer, then stood and listened.
Next: a version for one plant on a desk, so it can live in someone's home.

title: Tidal
description: A wall of light that slows its pulse to match the breathing of the people in front of it.

data.text: Sat on the subway platform at 1am and noticed the whole car exhale at once when the doors opened. What if a room could notice that? Not respond loudly. Just breathe back.

data.caption: First sketch. Wall of light, two people, the waves slow down when they slow down.

data.note: Calm technology as a frame: information that lives at the periphery and moves to the centre only when needed.

data.text: Resting breathing rate is roughly 12 to 20 breaths per minute. Slow-paced breathing guides usually target about 6. The wall should never lead faster than the slowest person in the room.

data.caption: Chest strap vs. 60GHz mmWave radar at 1.5m. Radar lags by about half a breath but no wearable needed.

data.text: Voice note: tried the webcam approach with pose tracking on shoulders. Works when people stand still, falls apart the second anyone talks or turns. Parking it.
Easing matters more than accuracy. A linear map from breath rate to wave speed feels mechanical. A 4 second smoothing window makes it feel like it is listening.
Final rig: 6 strips of WS2812B behind a frosted acrylic diffuser, ESP32 running FastLED, radar over serial. Teensy was overkill.

data.note: FastLED handles the LED timing so the ESP32 can spend its cycles on breath detection.

data.caption: Installed at the thesis show. People stayed longer than I expected. A few closed their eyes.

data.text: What I would change: the wall cannot tell two people apart, so it averages them. Next version should hold two rhythms at once and let them drift together.

title: Soft Machines
description: Knitted sensors that notice how they are being held.

data.text: Conductive yarn changes resistance when stretched. What if a scarf could tell a hug from a tug?
